payload.input:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Oil (lamp oil)

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In popular Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of the Holy Spirit — the inward, divine presence or empowering that cannot be borrowed or transferred and that sustains the believer's light/witness. In the Parable of the Ten Virgins this is typically preached as the indwelling Spirit (or, closely related, genuine spiritual life produced by the Spirit) that distinguishes true readiness for Christ's return from mere outward profession.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:1-13 (Parable of the Ten Virgins — the central lamp-oil text)",
    "Zechariah 4:1-6 (the golden lampstand fed by oil, interpreted 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit')",
    "Exodus 27:20-21 (pure oil to keep the tabernacle lamps burning continually)",
    "1 Samuel 16:13 (anointing oil linked with the Spirit coming upon David)",
    "Acts 10:38 (God 'anointed' Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power)",
    "1 John 2:20, 27 ('anointing' from the Holy One, commonly connected to the oil/Spirit link)",
    "Psalm 45:7 / Hebrews 1:9 ('oil of gladness' associated with divine anointing)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Good works, deeds of love, or the fruit of genuine discipleship — the classic Augustinian/patristic reading of the wise virgins' oil, sometimes tied to Matthew 5:14-16 (light shining through good works).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13",
        "Matthew 5:14-16",
        "Augustine's sermons on the Ten Virgins; echoed in medieval and some later exegesis"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Saving faith or grace — Reformation-era and later Protestant readings take the oil as true, living faith (or God's grace) versus empty profession.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13",
        "Ephesians 2:8-9 (grace/faith framing)",
        "Luther, Calvin, and later Protestant commentary traditions"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Spiritual preparedness/watchfulness with no fixed allegorical referent — many modern academic commentators argue the oil is simply a narrative device meaning 'readiness' for the delayed Parousia and should not be allegorized.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13 read in context of Matthew 24:36-25:46 (watchfulness discourse)",
        "Standard critical commentaries on Matthew (e.g., Davies-Allison, France, Hagner note caution against allegorizing)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The Word of God / knowledge of God as that which fuels the believer's light (lamp = Word, Psalm 119:105, so oil = what keeps the Word alive in the heart).",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 119:105",
        "Proverbs 6:23",
        "Matthew 25:1-13"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Personal righteousness or a testimony/relationship with Christ that cannot be borrowed — a reading emphasized in some traditions (notably Latter-day Saint teaching) and some evangelical preaching, focusing on the non-transferability of the oil.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13 (the wise cannot share their oil)",
        "LDS teaching (e.g., Spencer W. Kimball's 'drop by drop' exposition)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "There is a recognizable dominant strand — oil = Holy Spirit — that prevails in popular, devotional, Pentecostal/charismatic, and much evangelical teaching, grounded in the broader biblical association of anointing oil with the Spirit. However, this is not a settled scholarly consensus: the history of interpretation is genuinely divided (good works in Augustine and much patristic/medieval exegesis; faith/grace in Reformation exegesis; Holy Spirit in much modern preaching), and a large share of modern critical commentators decline to allegorize the oil at all, treating it as a figure for readiness. So the honest picture is: dominant popular meaning = Holy Spirit; academic consensus = deliberately non-allegorical 'preparedness'; historical alternatives remain live. Confidence is medium because prominence rankings among the alternatives vary by tradition and era."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "The Holy Spirit—especially the Spirit’s sustaining presence, power, and anointing—is the symbolic meaning most commonly assigned to lamp oil in Christian teaching.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Zechariah 4:1–6, 11–14: the lampstand’s continuing supply of oil is interpreted in connection with God’s Spirit: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.”",
    "1 Samuel 16:13: David is anointed with oil, and the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, establishing the standard association between oil and the Spirit.",
    "Isaiah 61:1 and Luke 4:18: anointing is directly associated with the Spirit of the Lord.",
    "Acts 10:38: God anoints Jesus “with the Holy Spirit and with power.”",
    "Matthew 25:1–13: the wise virgins’ possession of oil is frequently interpreted in Christian preaching as having the Holy Spirit or an inward spiritual life that sustains readiness for Christ’s return.",
    "Exodus 27:20–21 and Leviticus 24:1–4: pure oil continually maintains the sanctuary lamps, often used typologically for sustained spiritual illumination or the Spirit’s enabling presence."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Readiness, watchfulness, and persevering discipleship rather than a specific referent such as the Holy Spirit. On this reading, the oil in Matthew 25 functions narratively as what distinguishes those prepared for the bridegroom’s delayed arrival.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1–13, especially the concluding command, “Keep watch.”",
        "Matthew 24:42–51 and 25:14–30, whose surrounding parables emphasize faithful conduct during delay.",
        "Many historical-critical interpreters caution against assigning every detail of the parable a fixed allegorical equivalent."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Good works, obedience, or an enacted life of faith. The burning lamps represent visible discipleship sustained by righteous conduct.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 5:14–16 connects light with good works visible to others.",
        "Matthew 25:31–46, in the immediate broader context, emphasizes concrete acts of mercy.",
        "Early and later Christian allegorical readings sometimes identify the oil with works of love, mercy, or charity."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Divine grace, inward faith, or a genuine personal relationship with Christ—something spiritually necessary that cannot simply be borrowed from another person.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:8–12, where the foolish virgins cannot obtain what they lack in time and are not recognized by the bridegroom.",
        "Ephesians 2:8–10 and related theological syntheses are sometimes brought into the interpretation, though they do not directly define lamp oil."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Scripture or divine truth supplying spiritual illumination.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 119:105 calls God’s word a lamp and a light, although it does not identify the word as oil.",
        "Lamp and light imagery in Proverbs 6:23 is sometimes extended typologically to the oil that fuels the lamp."
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "No independent symbolic meaning: the oil is simply a necessary element of the story or cultic lamp equipment, while the symbolic force belongs to the whole lamp scene.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1–13 can be read without assigning a separate symbolic identity to the oil.",
        "Exodus 27:20–21 and Leviticus 24:1–4 primarily prescribe literal oil for sanctuary lamps."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Oil broadly has a well-established Christian association with the Holy Spirit because biblical anointing and the coming of the Spirit are repeatedly linked. Lamp oil specifically, especially in Matthew 25, has no fully settled symbolic interpretation. Popular preaching often identifies it with the Holy Spirit, while many exegetes regard preparedness or persevering faithfulness as the parable’s safer primary sense."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "The Holy Spirit (as the source of light, anointing, and spiritual empowerment)",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:1-13 (oil in the lamps of the wise virgins)",
    "Zechariah 4:1-14 (oil feeding the lampstand)",
    "Exodus 27:20-21 and Leviticus 24:1-4 (pure olive oil for the tabernacle lamp)",
    "1 Samuel 16:13 and related anointing texts linked to Spirit endowment"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Spiritual readiness, vigilance, or preparedness for Christ's return",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13 (contextual emphasis on the virgins' foresight)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Faith, grace, or personal piety that sustains spiritual life",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13 (oil as the 'fuel' distinguishing wise from foolish)",
        "Psalm 23:5"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Good works or righteous deeds that accompany faith",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13 (some patristic and moral readings)",
        "James 2:14-26 (works as evidence)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Joy or gladness",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 45:7 / Hebrews 1:9 (oil of gladness)",
        "Isaiah 61:3"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Across historic Christian teaching (patristic, medieval, Reformation, and modern evangelical/catholic sources) lamp oil is most consistently linked to the Holy Spirit, especially via the light motif and the parable of the virgins; secondary moral or preparatory readings of Matthew 25 remain common but do not displace the pneumatological consensus for oil as a biblical symbol."
}

BOOK ENTRY
Spirit-taught truth and correction received, kept, and worked into proven obedience — the tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit stored inwardly; light is that obedience made visible as an example to others.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: the Holy Spirit — anointing, consecration, and empowering.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ex 25:6; 27:20; Ps 141:5; Prov 21:20; 23:23; 27:5-9; Ezek 36:27; Zech 4:6-14; Matt 25:3-9; 5:16) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20, and The Anointing

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS

Exodus 27:20 — And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring thee pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always.

Zechariah 4:9 — The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you.

Matthew 25:8 — And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.
Matthew 25:9 — But the wise answered, saying, Not so; lest there be not enough for us and you: but go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

- MATCH: substantially the same meaning as the recognizable consensus.
- REFINED: compatible with the consensus but materially sharper, narrower,
  broader, or more precisely supported.
- DIVERGENT: contradicts or displaces a recognizable common interpretation.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus covers the book's central claim; the book
  stakes a meaning not represented by the blind responses.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
